Take the advice of creating a basic classroom structure, almost militaristic. We sit here, we open our books, we read aloud, we answer questions, etc. When it got really bad, I wrote our class rules on a large piece of paper and we started the class off by reciting them. Every. Day. When students would act up, I had desks that faced the back and extra packets. Offenders sat, facing the wall, working on the packet. If they continued to disrupt or be disrespectful, then you can send them out to the office WITH a packet and a referral. That looks much better to administration, and gives you accountability for their work.

Don't be lenient. Demand respect. When a student does not give it, have clear consequences. Focus on the ones who WANT to succeed, not the ones who will repeat the course.

I worked in an educational institution that implemented project-based learning school-wide, across different grades and subjects. In fact, we didn't really have traditional subjects. For one semester, students were presented with a big question, from which they chose a sub-question that addressed a part of that question, and then generated additional questions to help answer their sub-question.

It was quite chaotic, but a natural way to learn. It resembled a large research project. Students utilized the internet, gathered research, divided tasks, created outlines, and then used their findings to develop some form of presentation.

I observed that integrating mathematics was the most challenging aspect of this model. I believe the institution needed an educator who was well-versed in applying math in real-world contexts. Additionally, the school would have benefited from more structured workshops focused on math or writing skills. Nonetheless, it was an incredible experience that significantly influenced my approach to inquiry-based learning.

The primary issue I encountered was a lack of backward planning, or very minimal outlines of what we aimed to achieve. It was challenging to get the entire group to plan out a semester, which was essential! My suggestion would be to ensure that you thoroughly map it out. Create a basic outline with the benchmarks you want to achieve, and then consider the daily lessons necessary to guide students toward those benchmarks. The more effectively you plan, the more adaptable you can be.

For mathematics, if you can devise a real-world scenario or a tangible product that students can create, that will be invaluable for project-based learning. Students need a clear end goal for their projects, and it should be something that is always relevant and useful. Without that, students may lose interest.

This approach emphasizes viewing the classroom as a space to awaken individuals to their own oppression and motivate them to strive for social justice. In my thesis, I drew significant inspiration from a well-known scholar's theory of Big D Discourse. The core idea is that we all belong to various discourse communities, and our ability to navigate these communities determines our effectiveness as members. Conversely, failing to engage with the "language" of a community can lead to significant disadvantages. For instance, consider the recent discussions about educators from a country with a different educational focus coming to another country. The educational discourse in the latter often emphasizes standards and testing, which can create challenges for those unfamiliar with this approach. Even within the same country, the resurgence of project-based learning can leave traditional educators feeling out of place and struggling to engage with new methodologies in a system that is pushing for innovation.

I'm a huge discussion teacher, inspired by influential educational theorists. I want to know what learners get out of a text before I explain higher concepts. Literature is a personal experience, and what my learners derive from it is individualized. I don't need to start at the standards because I can adapt and embed them when necessary. The standards were born out of what we naturally do as educators!

I also switch seating for learners continually. Often they are in groups getting to know one another and leading their education in accordance with what a project asks them to answer. I dislike rows and asking for raised hands. I try not to have a "front" to the class. I aim to deconstruct the "standard" classroom so learners can also consider breaking their expectations of education and figure out how they learn best.

When it comes to navigating different discourses, I'm all about having learners engage with various perspectives. It aligns with the idea of becoming a social agent of your education.
